item.title: PM leads thousands in November 7 procession
item.description:
Walking on foot at the head of thousands of supporters, Prime Minister and BNP Chairman Tarique Rahman on Saturday turned National Revolution and Solidarity Day into a show of strength and a warning, vowing that the people would again give a “crushing response” to any conspiracy against Bangladesh’s democracy and sovereignty.
He warned that a group was once again conspiring to undermine Bangladesh’s sovereignty and revive the culture of “dummy elections”, but said the people would give them a strong response, as they had done in 1971, 1975 and 1990.
Tarique made the remarks at a brief rally in front of the BNP’s central office in Naya Paltan, Dhaka, marking National Revolution and Solidarity Day. He later led a colorful procession from Naya Paltan to Manik Mia Avenue, walking alongside party leaders and activists.
“Just as in the past, they are still engaged in conspiracies. Once again, they want to undermine Bangladesh’s sovereignty. They want to bring back the system of ‘dummy elections’,” the prime minister said.
“Just as we did in 1971, in 1990 and on November 7, 1975, we want to give them a crushing response once again. Let today’s November 7 procession be the day we fulfil that expectation. Let this procession be a day to protect Bangladesh’s independence and sovereignty,” he added.
Photo: PMO
Referring to the mass uprising of August 5, 2024, Tarique said the students and people had not only restored the country’s independence and sovereignty but had also driven the autocratic forces and conspirators out of power.
“Just as those forces were defeated on November 7, 1975, they were defeated again on August 5, 2024, through a movement involving the people,” he said.
The prime minister said a nation capable of achieving independence in 1971, staging the Sepoy-People’s Revolution in 1975 and bringing about the mass uprising in 2024 could never be subdued through conspiracies.
Tarique urged people to come forward to safeguard the democracy that, he said, had been established through the sacrifices of people during the mass uprising of August 5, 2024.
“Let us bring together all democracy-loving people of Bangladesh. Whether a conspiracy originates inside the country or outside it, we will collectively respond to all such attempts,” he said.
He added that no conspiracy could suppress the people who believe in democracy.
Photo: Ahadul Karim Khan/Dhaka Tribune
Addressing the thousands of party leaders and activists gathered in Naya Paltan, he asked: “Are you with us?” The crowd responded with applause and slogans.
Highlighting the significance of November 7, the prime minister said the day represented national unity, the protection of Bangladesh’s independence and sovereignty, and the freedom of expression of its people.
He also reiterated the slogan: “Not Delhi, not Pindi, nor any other country. Bangladesh comes first, Bangladesh for all.”
“Let us begin our revolution today,” he said.
After delivering his speech, Tarique joined the procession at around 3:30pm, leading thousands of party leaders and activists on foot.
The procession started in front of the BNP’s central office in Naya Paltan and passed through Kakrail intersection, the road beside the chief justice’s residence, the Ramna Park area, Hotel InterContinental intersection, Bangla Motor, Farmgate and Indira Road before reaching Manik Mia Avenue at around 4:30pm.
Photo: Ahadul Karim Khan/Dhaka Tribune
The prime minister walked the entire six-kilometer route alongside party leaders and activists. He wore a white half-sleeved shirt, grey trousers and navy-blue sneakers.
Thousands of people stood on both sides of the streets to catch a glimpse of him, while many others gathered on rooftops and balconies of nearby buildings. Tarique responded to their greetings with smiles and waves.
Leaders of the Jubo Dal, Swechchhasebak Dal, Krishak Dal and Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal were at the front of the procession, followed by senior BNP leaders, cabinet members and activists of the party’s associate organizations.
Additional Press Secretary to the Prime Minister Atikur Rahman Rumon described Tarique’s continuous six-kilometer walk as an unprecedented event in Bangladesh’s political history. He said the procession would inspire people in the journey towards rebuilding democracy.
Rumon also recalled that BNP founder and former president Ziaur Rahman had walked long distances while participating in canal excavation programs. He said Tarique maintained the same pace throughout the procession and encouraged other leaders to keep walking.
Photo: PMO
BNP leaders and activists from different parts of Dhaka and surrounding districts began gathering in Naya Paltan in small processions from around 12 noon on Saturday. As the day progressed, the area became increasingly crowded, with thousands of party leaders, activists and supporters gathered along the stretch from Kakrail intersection to Fakirerpool.
Many participants carried the national flag and placards featuring portraits of BNP founder Ziaur Rahman, former prime minister Khaleda Zia and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.
The colorful procession featured participants wearing caps and T-shirts of different colors, along with banners and festoons. The streets echoed with various slogans.
BNP Standing Committee members Mirza Abbas Uddin Ahmed, Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury, Salahuddin Ahmed and Abu Zafar Md Zahid Hossain, along with Acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi and other senior leaders, attended the program.
Photo: PMO
Other participants included BNP Vice-Chairmen Nurul Islam Moni and Ahmed Aazam Khan, adviser Zahir Uddin Swapon, Joint Secretaries General Khairul Kabir Khokon and Habib-un-Nabi Khan Sohel, Treasurer Rashiduzzaman Millat and Publicity Secretary Sultan Salauddin Tuku.
Tarique returned to Bangladesh on December 25, 2025, after spending around 17 years in London. Since his return, he has addressed several public rallies and political gatherings. However, Saturday’s program marked his participation in a BNP procession on the occasion of National Revolution and Solidarity Day.

item.title: Bus torched beneath metro rail station in Pallabi
item.description:
A bus operated by Bihanga Paribahan was set on fire beneath a metro rail station in the capital’s Pallabi area on Saturday night.
No casualties were reported.
The incident took place at around 10:15pm on November 7.
Pallabi Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Jalal Uddin said miscreants threw petrol at the bus in a bottle before setting it ablaze. The fire was brought under control shortly afterwards.
He said two rear seats of the bus were damaged in the fire. No one was injured as there were no passengers on board at the time.
The OC added that several miscreants arrived on motorcycles and carried out the attack. Police are examining CCTV footage from the scene and surrounding areas to identify and arrest those involved.

item.title: Sakhawat: Shaheed Zia introduced multi-party democracy
item.description:
Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain on Sunday said multi-party democracy was introduced in Bangladesh under the leadership of Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman.
"On November 7, 1975, at a critical juncture for the nation, Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman assumed responsibility for the country and played a pivotal role in steering Bangladesh out of a precarious political situation. Multi-party democracy was established under his leadership, safeguarding the nation's independence and sovereignty," said the minister.
"He will remain immortal in the nation's memory," he said, referring to National Revolution and Solidarity Day.
The minister made the remarks as the chief guest at a programme held at Belabo Upazila Parishad premises in Narsingdi to distribute humanitarian assistance, corrugated tin sheets and sewing machines among poor and underprivileged people.
Highlighting Ziaur Rahman's contributions, the minister said Bangladesh's independence and sovereignty would have faced grave risks had he not taken charge on November 7.
He added that Ziaur Rahman did not limit his role to declaring independence but also directly participated in the Liberation War as the commander of Z Force. He later guided the country's economic progress until his death, the minister said.
At the programme, the minister distributed Tk10,000 each among 90 underprivileged people as humanitarian assistance.
Another 56 beneficiaries received two bundles of corrugated tin sheets each, along with Tk6,000 each for house construction. Sewing machines were also distributed among 200 working women.
Officials of the upazila administration and leaders of different associate organisations of BNP in Belabo Upazila attended the programme.

item.title: Youth found dead at Madhya Badda
item.description:
A youth was found hanging from a ceiling fan at his home in Madhya Badda, Dhaka, on Saturday.
The deceased was identified as Sanjay Chandra Das, 34, son of the late Khir Mohan Chandra Das and resident of Madhya Badda.
He was rushed to the emergency department of Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH) around 6:30pm, where doctors declared him dead.
His nephew, Tushar Chandra Das, said Sanjay had been living in Germany before returning to Bangladesh six months ago to settle permanently.
He said Sanjay's marriage was being arranged and that he had visited a prospective bride's family earlier this week. The bride's family was scheduled to visit their home next Wednesday.
Tushar said Sanjay locked himself in his room on Saturday afternoon and allegedly hanged himself from a ceiling fan using a piece of cloth. Family members later broke down the door and rescued him.
However, relatives could not determine what prompted him to take his own life.
Inspector Habibur Rahman, in-charge of the DMCH police outpost, said the body had been kept at the hospital morgue and the relevant police station had been informed.

item.title: Authorities: No extra fee for HSC supplementary exam forms
item.description:
The Inter-Education Board Examination Controllers' Committee has instructed all educational institutions not to charge any additional fees from candidates in the name of filling out forms for the HSC and equivalent (supplementary) examinations.
Legal action will be taken against the heads of the concerned institutions and the institutions themselves for violating the directive.
The instruction was issued in an order published by the Inter-Education Board Examination Controllers' Committee recently.
The order said complaints had been received from various sources that additional fees were being collected from candidates in the name of filling out forms for the HSC and equivalent (supplementary) examinations.
In view of these complaints, the committee has clearly instructed that no additional fees can be collected from any candidate for filling out examination forms for the HSC and equivalent (supplementary) examinations.
The education boards have requested principals of all educational institutions at the HSC level to comply with the directive with due importance.

item.title: Defaced Tagore mural being restored in Khulna
item.description:
Khulna City Corporation (KCC) has begun repainting a mural of Rabindranath Tagore on a railway station wall along Jessore Road in the city after it was defaced with black ink on Friday.
The repainting work began on Saturday afternoon, said KCC Administrator Nazrul Islam Manju.
Earlier in the day, the KCC administrator inspected the defaced mural at Shibbari intersection.
Condemning the incident, he said smearing ink on the portrait of Rabindranath Tagore was an act of disrespect and malice.
He said action would be taken against those responsible for the incident.
While everyone is entitled to their personal views, their expression should not involve disrespecting others, creating public unrest or inciting hatred, he said.
"Erasing an image does not negate the person it represents," he remarked, urging everyone to remain vigilant against attempts to target works of art out of political vendetta.
Lokman Hossain, officer-in-charge of Khulna Sadar Police Station, said it was not immediately clear who had defaced the mural or when the incident occurred, as businesses on the opposite side of the road were closed on Friday.
Police have launched an investigation into the incident, he added.
The defacement came to light on Friday afternoon when local residents noticed that black ink had been smeared over Tagore's face in the mural. Two posters bearing the headline "Opposition to the establishment of Dhaka University" had also been put up on either side of the portrait.
As part of a KCC initiative to beautify the city ahead of a visit by Tarique Rahman, murals of eminent national figures were painted on walls at different locations across Khulna.
The murals feature portraits of world-renowned poet Rabindranath Tagore, National Poet Kazi Nazrul Islam, former Prime Minister Begum Khaleda Zia, martyred President Ziaur Rahman and poet Michael Madhusudan Dutt.
They also depict the history, heritage and culture of Khulna.

item.title: Man killed, 10 injured in Sylhet clash over mosque committee
item.description:
A man was killed and at least 10 others injured in a clash over a long-standing dispute involving a mosque committee in Lakshmipur village of Sylhet's Dakshin Surma upazila on Friday.
The deceased was identified as Md. Geda Mia, 65, a local arbitration figure from Lakshmipur village under Tetli Union.
The injured were admitted to Sylhet MAG Osmani Medical College Hospital for treatment.
Locals said Geda Mia's family had been involved in a long-running dispute over the mosque committee with a rival group led by Alauddin and Elias.
On Friday evening, Alauddin, Elias and their accomplices allegedly attacked Geda Mia's house and looted the house of his son, Kamal.
When Geda Mia tried to resist them, the attackers hacked him with sharp weapons, leaving him dead on the spot, locals said.
Tetli Union Parishad Chairman Oliur Rahman visited the spot along with police and helped arrange the transfer of the injured to hospital.
Ashraful Islam, officer-in-charge (OC) of South Surma Police Station, said the body was handed over to the family after an autopsy. Efforts are underway to arrest those involved in the attack, he added.

item.title: Woman found hanging in Demra
item.description:
Police recovered the hanging body of a 40-year-old woman from a house in South Hajinagar area of Demra, Dhaka, on Saturday.
The deceased, identified as Josna Begum, was found hanging inside a tin-shed house at around 11:30am. Her body was later sent to the Dhaka Medical College Hospital morgue for an autopsy.
Josna was the daughter of Abu Kalam from Krishnanagar village in Nabinagar upazila of Brahmanbaria. She lived in Demra with her husband, Md Faruk, a bus driver, and their 4 children.
Demra police station Sub-Inspector Mohammad Saddam Hossain said police received information about the incident at around 12:30pm and recovered her body from a room in the house.
He said relatives claimed that Josna had an argument with her husband over a family dispute and subsequently hanged herself using a scarf tied to a ceiling beam. However, the exact cause of death would be determined after the autopsy report is received.
Josna's husband, Faruk, who works as a bus driver for Alif Paribahan, said: “My wife was a homemaker. Following an argument over domestic matters, she became upset and died by suicide by hanging herself.”

item.title: Prisoner dies at DMCH after falling ill in jail
item.description:
A prisoner at Dhaka Central Jail in Keraniganj died at Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH) on Saturday morning. The deceased was identified as Md Shamim, 32.
Prison guards brought Shamim to the DMCH emergency department in an ailing condition on Saturday morning. After examination, on-duty doctors declared him dead at 10:20am.
Inspector Md Habibur Rahman of the DMCH police outpost said Shamim hailed from Dhamrai in Savar. However, the case in which he had been detained could not be confirmed immediately.
He added that the body had been kept at the hospital morgue for an autopsy.

9th teacher recruitment exam to be held in 3 stages, syllabus may change
item.description:
The Ninth Teacher Recruitment Examination, organised by the Non-Government Teachers’ Registration and Certification Authority (NTRCA), may take place in December.

The NTRCA plans to hold the examination after completing the ongoing viva voce examinations for the recruitment of heads and assistant heads of educational institutions.

Meanwhile, the examination format for the Ninth Teacher Recruitment Examination may undergo changes. In addition to the existing preliminary and viva voce examinations, a written examination may also be introduced. However, the final decision will depend on amendments to the relevant regulations.

According to NTRCA sources, the Ninth Teacher Recruitment Examination may take place in December. The syllabus for the new recruitment examination may also be revised.

9th teacher recruitment exam: NTRCA gives timeline

Syllabus and marks distribution

Under the proposed examination format, candidates may have to sit for examinations in three stages. The first stage will consist of a 100-mark multiple-choice question (MCQ) examination lasting one hour.

Candidates will receive one mark for each correct answer, while 0.25 marks will be deducted for each incorrect answer. The pass mark will be 40 per cent.

Candidates who pass the preliminary examination will be eligible to sit for a 100-mark written examination, which will last three hours. Those who pass the written examination will then have to attend a 20-mark viva voce examination.

The proposed syllabus for the preliminary examination includes four subjects: Bengali, English, Mathematics and General Knowledge. Each subject will carry 25 marks, making the examination worth a total of 100 marks.

However, the examination format, marks distribution and syllabus will be finalised after the relevant regulations have been amended.

According to NTRCA sources, viva voce examinations for the recruitment of heads and assistant heads of educational institutions are currently underway. These examinations are scheduled to conclude on 9 December.

The Ninth Teacher Recruitment Examination may take place afterwards. However, the final decision on the examination will depend on approval from the Ministry of Education.

Recruitment begins for previously omitted candidates in primary school teacher posts

This year's examination will introduce a major change to the recruitment process. For the first time, the registration examination will lead directly to recruitment rather than merely assessing candidates' eligibility.

For this reason, it will be designated the Ninth Teacher Recruitment Examination instead of continuing the previous sequence as the 19th Teacher Registration Examination.

The NTRCA last published a notification for the 18th Teacher Registration Examination on 4 November 2023. The preliminary examination took place in March 2024, approximately four months later.

After a lengthy interval, arrangements are now being made to hold a new teacher recruitment examination.

item.title: Have a degree but no job? Don’t lose hope
item.description:
It was 2004. I had just graduated in computer engineering from a university in the United States. My head was full of dreams: I would get a good job, become financially independent and start working towards the rest of my life plans. I began sending my résumé to different organisations several months before graduation. But despite submitting one application after another, I heard nothing about a job.

At the time, I was an international student in the United States. If I failed to find a job related to my field of study within a specified period, I would have to return home empty-handed. And there was another worry even before that: how would I pay the rent? How would I put food on the table?

With little choice, I took a job at a pizza shop to cover my expenses. I spent all day making pizzas, washing dishes and wiping tables. There is nothing undignified about earning an honest living. But every now and then, I wondered what all those years of education had been for.

Eventually, I decided that if I could not find a job, I might as well return to studying. I sat for the GRE and applied for admission to graduate programmes. Every day, I would sit in front of my computer, refreshing my email inbox. Would I ever be free of this uncertainty?

Twenty-two years later, in 2026, when I think about the young people in Bangladesh looking for jobs, I am reminded of those days. Today, many have degrees but no jobs. Some families have taken out loans to finance their education, while others have shouldered the responsibility of supporting their younger siblings' studies. And then there are the familiar questions from relatives: “Any news? Have you found a job?” The question is simple enough; answering it is much harder.

Doubting one's own abilities, worrying about the future and feeling left behind while everyone around you moves ahead—these are feelings I know all too well.

We are quick to advise unemployed young people: work harder, acquire more skills. Hard work and skills are certainly important. But we also need to consider other factors. According to the Bangladesh Labour Force Survey 2024, the unemployment rate among university graduates is around 13.5 per cent. When so many young people cannot find jobs, it is only reasonable to ask: is the problem simply a lack of qualifications and experience? Opportunities for higher education are expanding, but are suitable jobs being created at the same pace?

Artificial intelligence, or AI, has added another layer of anxiety. Tasks that people once performed—writing reports, developing code and analysing data—can now have their first drafts produced by AI in an instant. Does that mean everything we have learnt so far will become worthless?

It is not an unreasonable question. Researchers at Stanford University in the United States have found that employment among young workers has declined relatively more in occupations highly exposed to AI. Of course, AI alone cannot be held responsible for all of this. But it is worth thinking about. Young employees usually gain experience by starting with small tasks. If AI takes over those very tasks, where will newcomers learn? And without experience, how will they get good jobs? It is a vicious cycle.

People's anxieties about new technology are nothing new. Around 2,500 years ago, the Greek philosopher Socrates, as recorded in Plato's writings, expressed concern that if people began writing everything down, they would stop exercising their memory. After all, they would no longer need to remember things themselves. The irony is that we still know about Socrates' concern today precisely because Plato wrote it down.

Let me give another example. In the 1990s, when everyone used landlines, we knew the phone numbers of many people by heart. After mobile phones arrived, many of us can no longer even remember the phone numbers of our own family members. But does that mean our ability to remember has declined?

Or consider GPS. In the past, finding your way around an unfamiliar city meant consulting a map or asking passers-by for directions. Now we simply follow the instructions on our phones to reach our destinations. Some research has also suggested that excessive use of GPS may weaken our ability to navigate independently.

In other words, technology makes our lives easier, but in return, we may practise certain skills less. Does that mean we have stopped writing, using mobile phones or relying on GPS? No. Instead, our habits and ways of working have changed alongside technology. We need to look at AI in the same way. We should not be afraid simply because machines are taking over some human tasks. We also need to consider how technology is enabling people to do things they could not do before, or that once took them much longer.

A 2025 analysis by the International Labour Organisation says that nearly one in four jobs worldwide could be transformed by AI. In most cases, however, jobs are more likely to change in nature than disappear altogether. But simply saying that the nature of work will change is hardly reassuring. What guarantees that everyone will have equal access to the new opportunities? Those who get the chance to learn new technologies will move ahead. Others may fall further behind. So rather than denying the change, we need to prepare for it.

I have been researching the relationship between people and technology for many years. In 2011, I gave an enthusiastic speech at a conference about the potential of artificial intelligence. After the talk, someone approached me and spoke about the difficulties he faced in social interactions. He then asked, “If science does not help people, what is the point of doing science?” His words had a profound impact on me.
Researchers like us often get caught up in how intelligent a new technology is and how quickly it can work. But that person's question reminded me that what matters even more than how intelligent a machine becomes is this: whom does it actually benefit?

Drawing on that experience, I want to tell today's young people something. It is not enough to learn how to use AI to generate polished answers. You also need to understand which questions should be asked, where an answer might be wrong and whose life that answer could improve.

Perhaps the most valuable skill of the future will not simply be knowing the answers, but knowing how to ask the right questions. AI may write the code, but that does not automatically make the software secure. Giving advice to farmers does not necessarily make it suitable for Bangladesh's soil and climate. Organising information for a patient does not make it a substitute for a doctor's judgement. These tasks require subject knowledge and an understanding of people's realities. They also require empathy, ethics and a willingness to take responsibility for one's work.

So what can those who are still studying, or searching for jobs after earning a degree, do? I believe they do not need to land a job at a major organisation to prove their abilities. They can start on a small scale. If you are an accounting student, develop a simple system to organise the accounts of a small shop in your neighbourhood. If you are a journalism student, fact-check AI-generated news and show where it gets things wrong. If you study computer science, build something that genuinely helps a farmer in a village or a person with a disability.

Good internet access, training and employment opportunities need to reach different parts of the country. If the benefits of technology remain limited to a few people in cities, inequality will only increase.

But building something is not enough. Put it in the hands of the people it is intended for. Ask whether they can use it. If something goes wrong, fix it. Then build a portfolio documenting your work and the evidence of what you have achieved. Not every initiative will lead to a job. But in your next interview, instead of simply saying, “I can do this”, you will be able to say, “Here, I have done it.” That is no small difference.

This does not mean that degrees are no longer necessary. Without a strong foundation, how will we identify AI's mistakes? The fundamental knowledge we acquire at university helps us evaluate new technologies, question them and make corrections when necessary.

However, after all this, we must not end up placing the entire burden on young people's shoulders. Universities, the government and employers also have responsibilities. University curricula need to be more closely linked to real-world problems. Technology and workplaces are changing, but how much is the gap narrowing between what students learn and what they actually need to do at work?

Employers, too, need to create more internship opportunities for newcomers. If everyone wants experienced employees, where will newcomers gain experience? And opportunities must not remain confined to Dhaka. Good internet access, training and employment opportunities need to reach different parts of the country. If the benefits of technology remain limited to a few people in cities, inequality will only increase.

I also have a request for families and society. Do not judge someone by their first job—or by their unemployment. Young people need advice, certainly, but they also need some reassurance and an opportunity. Instead of asking “Have you found a job?” every day, sometimes asking “How can I help?” may be far more useful.

When I was working at the pizza shop, I had no idea that one day I would teach at a university and conduct research. At the time, I could not even see what lay ahead of me. I am not suggesting that everyone's life will unfold the way mine did. Some people's paths are much harder. Some may not even have the opportunity to return to their studies, as I did. So I do not want to offer the hollow reassurance that “everything will work out if you just keep trying”. But I can say this much: the situation you are in today is not the final chapter of your life. Change direction if necessary, seek help from others and keep learning. If one approach does not work, try another.

Dear Gen Z friends, your degree is an achievement. But it is not your entire identity. And failing to find a job, or struggling to get one, is not the final verdict on your abilities either. Standing in that pizza shop one day, I too thought everything was over. Looking back now, I realise that it was only a difficult chapter. The real story was yet to come.

Your story is only just beginning.

*Ehsan Hoque is a professor of computer science at the University of Rochester, USA

item.title: No question of emotion over Sheikh Hasina’s return, we will apply the law: Law minister
item.description:
Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Md Asaduzzaman has said the government is following legal procedures to bring ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina back to Bangladesh.

He said, “Whatever legal measures are required regarding Sheikh Hasina, we are executing them through due process. We will deal with the matter in accordance with the law. You will see that when we take any action, there will be no question of emotion. The point is that I will apply the law.”

Home Ministry asked to take control of properties owned by Sheikh Hasina, Asaduzzaman

The minister made the remarks on Sunday morning after the inaugural session of a workshop on ‘Integrity in Judicial Proceedings’ at a hotel in the capital. The workshop was organised by Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB). TIB Executive Director Iftekharuzzaman was also present there.

After the inaugural session, journalists asked the law minister whether the government would pursue a legal battle in an Indian court to bring Sheikh Hasina back.

In response, the minister said, “That is a matter for the Indian government. We have made a request to them under the prisoner exchange agreement. If they hand her over to us, we will follow due process and bring her under the law as required.”

If Sheikh Hasina returns to the country, she will face justice, not mob violence: Prime Minister’s Adviser

The government has referred to the prisoner exchange agreement, but Sheikh Hasina is not being held as a prisoner in India. India describes her as a state guest.

When asked what would happen in that case, Md Asaduzzaman said, “To me, she is a criminal. She is a convicted criminal under a verdict by our tribunal—that is her identity to us. … What they (India) say is not the deciding factor. She was tried in an open court in our country.”

item.title: Braille printer for visually impaired, Tk 500,000-device available for Tk 28,000
item.description:
Siddharth Mistri is a student in the Department of Bangla at the University of Chittagong. He has been visually impaired since birth. After overcoming numerous challenges, he secured the opportunity to study at the university. He often has to prepare his own notes and study materials to meet his academic needs.

While others can easily print PDF or Word files and organise their study materials, the process is not so straightforward for him. He needs a specialised printer to print text in Braille, the system designed for visually impaired people, but such printers are extremely expensive.

Considering the difficulties faced by visually impaired students like Siddharth, Professor Md Ahsanullah of the Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering at Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology (CUET) had taken the initiative to develop a Braille printer.

A team of CUET students, known as 'Sync Robotics', has now turned his long-standing idea into reality. With Professor Ahsanullah’s guidance, they have developed a compact Braille printer named 'Sync V-1'.

Some private organisations import Braille books from abroad and produce books according to specific requirements. The printing machines they use cost more than Tk 10 million (1 crore). However, people in Bangladesh have virtually no opportunity to produce or print Braille text for personal use.

They built the device at a cost of just Tk 28,000 as an alternative to conventional Braille printers available in international markets, which cost around Tk 500,000.

Under the guidance of Professor Md Ahsanullah, fourth-year student Sourav Tarafdar from CUET’s Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering led the team behind the Braille printer. He was joined by Ifaz Hossain, a third-year student in the Department of Petroleum and Mining Engineering, and Imam Rashid, a first-year student in the Department of Civil Engineering.

xFusion Tech Day – Bangladesh highlights AI-driven innovation, enterprise infrastructure and next-generation technology solutions

The idea dates back nearly 20 years

The Braille system uses raised dots on paper to represent letters and words. Visually impaired people can read them by feeling the dots with their fingertips.

Producing these dots through conventional methods is time-consuming and labour-intensive. Modern Braille printers, meanwhile, are large and expensive. As a result, many people cannot afford to purchase these machines for personal use.

Professor Ahsanullah began considering the issue around 2005. He explored ways to develop this type of printer at a lower cost. At the time, he and Jahangir Alam, a teacher in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering, began research into Bengali Braille technology.

Their goal was to develop a technology for writing in Braille in the Bengali language. They also published a research paper on the subject. However, publishing the paper did not end Professor Ahsanullah’s efforts. He wanted to turn the research concept into a practical device.

Professor Ahsanullah said, “Our main objective was to make this printer accessible to everyone. It would be portable, compact and easy to use. We also considered incorporating voice support and keyboard sounds so that a visually impaired person could edit text and print it independently.”

Siddharth Mistri, visually impaired student, University of Chittagong We had to write everything by hand. Very little work is done to address the needs of visually impaired people like us. From that perspective, this is a major innovation for us. Compared with conventional printers, it is easier to use and more user-friendly.

Professor Ahsanullah said that the availability of Braille books in Bangladesh remained limited. He learnt that Dhaka University previously had a Braille printer donated by the Netherlands Government, but the machine was no longer operational.

Some private organisations import Braille books from abroad and produce books according to specific requirements.

The printing machines they use cost more than Tk 10 million (1 crore). However, people in Bangladesh have virtually no opportunity to produce or print Braille text for personal use.

Type and print directly in Braille

Users can operate Sync V-1 through dedicated software. When they type text in Bengali or English into the software, it automatically converts the text into Braille characters. They then insert a sheet of paper into the printer, which embosses the text in Braille dots. This eliminates the need to write Braille manually.

Users can also print text extracted from various file formats, including PDF and Word documents, rather than just typed text. The device currently supports Bengali and English.

Professor Ahsanullah said that further software development could make Braille printing available in other languages as well.

One of the device’s key advantages over conventional Braille printers is its compact size and portability. Users can carry it with them according to their needs and print materials whenever required.

Professor Ahsanullah said, “Conventional Braille printers available abroad can cost between USD 2,500 and USD 5,000, or even more. Our aim was to develop an affordable device that individuals could use themselves. Our primary objective is to make educational materials more accessible to visually impaired people.”

Visually impaired students’ reactions to the device

Two visually impaired students from the University of Chittagong have already tested the device. One of them is Siddharth Mistri. Pointing out that conventional Braille printers are beyond the reach of ordinary people, he said, “We had to write everything by hand. Very little work is done to address the needs of visually impaired people like us. From that perspective, this is a major innovation for us. Compared with conventional printers, it is easier to use and more user-friendly.”

The other user, Akash Das, also appreciated the device’s portability and practical features. He said, “The device is small and lightweight, so it is easy to carry. Its Braille dots are also clear, making the text easier to read. However, a few more refinements could make it even more effective.”

Recognition at the national level

The initiative to develop an affordable Braille printer has already received national recognition. Competing against 355 projects, 'Sync V-1' emerged as the champion at the Bangladesh ICT and Innovation Awards 2026.

Of the projects submitted this year, 118 were shortlisted for the final evaluation. Ultimately, nine projects were declared champions in different categories. 'Sync V-1' won in the Student—Tertiary, Inclusion and Public Service category.

Alongside this recognition, the team has also earned an opportunity to showcase its innovation internationally. As the winning project, 'Sync V-1' has been nominated to represent Bangladesh at the APICTA Awards 2026.

Professor Md Ahsanullah, Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, CUETOur main objective was to make this printer accessible to everyone. It would be portable, compact and easy to use. We also considered incorporating voice support and keyboard sounds so that a visually impaired person could edit text and print it independently.

Sourav Tarafdar, who leads the team, told Prothom Alo, “A country truly progresses when the knowledge and innovations developed in its laboratories do not remain confined to research papers but are translated into practical solutions that make a difference to people's lives. Our Braille printer also began as a research project. Our goal now is to take it beyond the laboratory and make it available to people as an affordable, accessible product that can be manufactured locally.”

DUCSU: Visually impaired Faruk wants Braille vote in national polls too

In his view, making Braille technology more accessible to visually impaired people would not only expand their educational opportunities but also facilitate skills development and future employment.

However, moving from the research stage to commercial production requires the right partners and investors.

With the necessary support, the team hopes to increase production and make the technology available to more visually impaired people across the country.

The innovators do not intend to stop at developing the printer. They plan to increase its printing speed, introduce wireless connectivity and make it compatible with more languages in the future.

According to Professor Ahsanullah, it would also be possible to incorporate a feature that prints conventional Bengali or English text alongside the Braille version. This would allow visually impaired students who write their answers in Braille to produce a conventional text version at the same time. As a result, they would have less need to rely on someone else to write their answers during examinations.

item.title: Sylhet Test: Taijul, Miraz strike, but West Indies take 98-run lead
item.description:
CRICKET-BAN-WIS-TEST

West Indies scored 121 runs in 30 overs and lost two wickets in the first session of the fourth day of the Sylhet Test, extending their lead over Bangladesh to 98 runs.

At lunch, West Indies were 128 for 2 in their second innings. Bangladesh’s spinners took both wickets, with Taijul Islam dismissing Joshua Da Silva for 36 and Mehidy Hasan Miraz removing half-centurion Brandon King for 61.

Hridoy's incredible batting puts Bangladesh in the lead

West Indies began the day at 7 without loss, still 16 runs behind Bangladesh. They made a brisk start, reaching 56 without loss after 14 overs. By the end of the first hour, they had scored 59 runs without losing a wicket, taking their lead to 36.

King brought up his sixth half-century in Test cricket, having remained unbeaten on 81 in the second innings of the Mirpur Test. He reached 61 off 79 balls before Miraz ended his innings.

The off-spinner bowled outside the off stump, and the ball drifted as King moved forward to defend. It took the outside edge and was caught by Najmul Hossain Shanto at slip.

Earlier, Taijul had given Bangladesh their first breakthrough of the innings, trapping Da Silva lbw for 36. Taijul had gone wicketless in the second innings of the Mirpur Test and in the first innings of this match.

Hodge remained unbeaten on 30 at the end of the session, helping West Indies maintain their scoring rate. The visitors added 121 runs in the session at more than four runs an over.

Hridoy makes history with maiden Test double century

Bangladesh had finished the third day with a 23-run first-innings lead, thanks to an unbeaten 242 from Towhid Hridoy. Bangladesh were all out for 386 in reply to West Indies’ first-innings total of 356.

Brief scores

West Indies: 356 and 128/2 (Brandon King 61, Joshua Da Silva 36, Hodge 30*; Mehidy Hasan Miraz 1/30, Taijul Islam 1/37).

Bangladesh: 386.

West Indies lead by 98 runs.

item.title: Pori Moni served legal notice demanding unconditional apology over court incident
item.description:
A Supreme Court lawyer has sent a legal notice to actress Pori Moni, asking her to issue a written, unconditional apology for an incident that took place on the court premises on Thursday, 5 November. The notice asks Pori Moni to apologise within seven days.

Apart from Pori Moni, the notice was also sent to the president and general secretary of the Bangladesh Film Artistes’ Association. Supreme Court lawyer Khandaker Hasan Shahriar told Prothom Alo that notices were sent by registered post to all three this morning, Sunday.

Journalist Robiul denies touching allegation, says Pori Moni snatched his phone

The notice asks Pori Moni to refrain entirely in future from all forms of obscene language or dialogue, threats, obscene acting, gestures and dancing, as well as anything else that has no artistic or educational value.

Addressing the president and general secretary of the Bangladesh Film Artistes’ Association, the legal notice says they must issue a show-cause notice to Pori Moni and take necessary disciplinary action against her within seven days of receiving it. Otherwise, the person who issued the notice will take the necessary legal steps under the present laws.

The legal notice alleges that Pori Moni surrendered to the court and secured bail in a case filed by businessman Nasir Uddin Mahmud. That day, at around 11:40 am, as she got out of her car and headed towards the courtroom, a scuffle broke out between her security guards and journalists who tried to take photographs and videos of her.

‘How dare he touch me!’ Enraged Pori Moni at court premises

At the time, Pori Moni snatched the mobile phone of a multimedia reporter from the newspaper Samakal. Security guards accompanying her also broke his tripod. Several media reporters were injured in the scuffle on the court premises that day. A plaintiff named Sujan Chandra Mani Das was also left injured. News reports said that he suffered a head injury and was bleeding.

Ensuring everyone's safety on court premises is the responsibility of the state and the administration. Therefore, no one is legally entitled to use a team of personal security guards to control the environment at a court or display physical force there.

Pori Moni granted bail on Tk 500 bond

According to the legal notice, Pori Moni later left the court premises. She then charged towards Samakal multimedia reporter Robiul Hossain, whose right hand is congenitally smaller than his left and has three missing fingers, leaving him unable to carry out normal activities with that hand.

Pori Moni hurled obscene abuse at him and openly threatened to kill him. Video footage of the incident has been broadcast by the media.

The notice states that such behaviour by Pori Moni towards a professional journalist is not merely an attack on his professional dignity; it also poses a threat to the environment necessary for independent journalism and the media to perform their duties. Such controversial conduct is in no way expected from a film actress like Pori Moni.

item.title: Sovereign AI ambition meets technical reality
item.description:
The government’s ambition to build a sovereign "Bangla Large Language Model (LLM)" has gained renewed momentum within official policymaking circles.
Spearheaded by the ICT Division and administrative stakeholders, the state plan envisions setting up high-performance computing nodes centered at the National Data Center in Kaliakair, supported by eight regional data centers across divisional headquarters.
The state's rationale frames local model development as a prerequisite for digital sovereignty, cultural preservation, and linguistic inclusion.
However, tech industry analysts, machine learning researchers, and software architects are raising critical questions about the technical premises and financial feasibility of state-funded foundational AI model creation.
While public narrative frequently treats AI models as discrete, language-bound software systems, modern foundational engineering reveals a very different landscape—one where direct government intervention risks creating a costly, redundant public asset rather than a useful technological utility.
In machine learning architecture, language-bound AI is a conceptual contradiction.
Neural networks do not process human vocabulary, syntax, or grammar in isolation; they function by converting input tokens into multi-dimensional vector embeddings within a shared mathematical concept space.
Modern foundational architectures process semantic logic, contextual connections, and structural patterns across dozens of human languages simultaneously.
State-funded plans to create a brand-new foundational model exclusively for Bangla misinterpret how global models function.
Frontier LLMs do not need to be rebuilt from scratch to comprehend Bengali. Massive open-source models—ranging from 24 billion to 64 billion parameters—already exist freely in the global developer ecosystem.
These platforms have already ingested vast swathes of open-web Bengali text during their multi-trillion-token pre-training phases.
Replicating this core architecture domestically adds zero foundational value while requiring computational infrastructure that costs billions of dollars—a scale of ongoing capital expenditure visible in the quarterly financial reports of global technology conglomerates like Google, Meta, and Anthropic.
Grounded integration
A significant volume of Bengali knowledge remains outside the digital realm—confined to printed literature, historical manuscripts, regional archives, and library collections across the country.
However, digitizing this material does not necessitate training a new foundation model from scratch.
To incorporate offline archives, the industry standard is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).
Under a RAG pipeline, physical documents are scanned, digitized, vectorized, and stored in a searchable database.
When a user asks a question, the system retrieves relevant historical context from local records and feeds it directly into an existing open-source LLM.
This delivers domain-specific accuracy without altering the underlying model parameters.
Similarly, regional accents and localized spoken dialects—such as Noakhali, Chattogram, or Sylheti—require targeted speech-to-text (STT) and fine-tuning datasets rather than foundational architecture redesigns.
Extending existing models to handle local vocal nuances is an incremental fine-tuning layer, not a ground-up engineering task.
Administrative limits and procurement hazards
Past industrial endeavors demonstrate that direct state execution in consumer or high-tech manufacturing struggles with rapid innovation cycles.
When deep-tech initiatives fall under conventional administrative frameworks, project implementation often shifts from software engineering toward traditional bureaucracy: tenders, procurement cycles, contractor allocations, and physical infrastructure management.
Instead of yielding agile, market-ready technology, direct state management risks creating over-budget and under-utilized assets—much like previous state technology assembly initiatives that struggled to find commercial adoption against global private competition.
Lessons from Google Bard
The global evolution of Natural Language Processing (NLP) demonstrates how multi-lingual models acquire non-English capabilities natively.
When Google introduced Bard (now Gemini), computer scientists noted that the system began demonstrating fluency in low-resource languages, including Bengali, through a phenomenon known as "emergent property."
By training deep transformer layers on massive multi-lingual datasets, the model independently maps linguistic structures, semantic relationships, and cross-lingual concepts.
By anchoring low-resource data against high-resource language vectors, global models developed Bengali comprehension organically through scale rather than through isolated, localized manual programming.
Strategic alternatives
Rather than allocating capital toward building redundant core models, experts suggest a pragmatic shift in state policy:
Evaluating the state-led Bangla AI push
Category
Pros (State-Led Native Model Push)
Cons (Technical & Financial Drawbacks)
Data & Sovereignty
Direct national administrative oversight over local citizen data and public service integration.
Redundant, as open-source multi-lingual models already process public Bengali text securely on local servers.
Resource Allocation
Allocates public funding toward national technology infrastructure and local data center expansion.
High financial burden; foundational pre-training costs billions in compute, duplicating existing global open-source work.
Execution Risk
Creates a centralized government roadmap for public-sector digitalization.
Vulnerable to administrative procurement delays, tender inefficiencies, and fast technical obsolescence.
Linguistic Scope
Encourages systematic digitization of physical Bengali archives and national literary collections.
Inefficient path for software delivery; RAG pipelines and model fine-tuning achieve identical domain accuracy at a fraction of the cost.

item.title: The future of 60m button phones in Bangladesh
item.description:
The telecommunications landscape in Bangladesh is heading toward a massive structural shift. The Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission (BTRC) has outlined a definitive roadmap to completely phase out 2G technology by December 2029.
While telecom operators have welcomed the decision as a necessary step toward modernizing digital infrastructure, the move raises serious questions about the fate of roughly 60 million traditional button phones currently in use across the country.
To ensure a managed transition away from legacy technology, BTRC has established a series of strict deadlines leading up to the final network shutdown:
Industry estimates indicate that about 65% of locally produced handsets are still basic 2G feature phones, typically priced around Tk950 to Tk1,000.
In contrast, affordable 4G smartphones generally start at a much higher price point of around Tk9,500.
Because the vast majority of existing button phones do not support VoLTE (Voice over LTE) technology, millions of low-income and rural consumers face a steep financial hurdle to stay connected once the network is retired.
Experts and local manufacturing representatives have emphasized that restricting 2G devices must be balanced with practical alternatives—such as government-backed initiatives for ultra-low-cost smartphones or accessible installment facilities—to prevent economic strain on lower-income populations and to avoid flooding the market with illegal devices.
Major mobile network operators, including Grameenphone, Robi, and Banglalink, have strongly endorsed the transition.
Industry leaders noted that retiring outdated 2G infrastructure will allow operators to redirect critical spectrum resources, significantly boost data network capacity, and deliver higher-quality mobile internet services nationwide as digital connectivity becomes the primary focus of the telecommunications sector.

West Indies focused on piling lead, not setting a target: Hodge
item.description:
CRICKET-BAN-WIS-TEST

West Indies batter Kavem Hodge said his team would continue to pile on the lead rather than set a fixed target, as they tightened their grip on the second and final Test against Bangladesh at Sylhet International Cricket Stadium today, Sunday.

Hodge, who struck an unbeaten century to put West Indies in control, said the wicket remained good for batting and the team would assess the situation before deciding how far they wanted to go on the fifth day.

“It’s a pretty good wicket. Tomorrow we’ll assess and see what’s the best score, what’s the best total, and what’s the best tempo on this wicket. But as of now, we’re just trying to keep piling on the lead,” Hodge told newspersons after the day’s play.

West Indies reached 345-3 at stumps on Day 4, stretching their overall lead to 315 runs and putting themselves in a strong position to push for a series sweep.

Hodge who was not out on 140 said his century was particularly satisfying as he managed to contribute at a crucial stage after failing to make a significant impact in the opening Test in Dhaka.

“I got a start in the first game in Dhaka, but obviously I didn’t get the results that I would have loved to. It’s always nice to contribute to the team. So it was really good to put on some runs for the team in a situation like that where the game was evenly poised,” he said.

Hodge said Towhid Hridoy’s remarkable 242 not out for Bangladesh had inspired the West Indies batters to believe they could produce similar performances on a batting-friendly surface.

“Anybody who had the opportunity to witness that would have appreciated the skill and the power of such an innings, regardless of the opponent. It was just proof that the wicket is really good. I think the notion was, if he could do it, why can’t we do it? And it turned out to be the exact same thing,” he said.

Asked whether West Indies were looking to bat for a draw rather than force a result, Hodge dismissed the suggestion, saying both teams were simply trying to put themselves in the best possible position.

Looking ahead to the final day, Hodge identified spin bowling as a potentially decisive factor, admitting that Bangladesh’s spinners had already managed to extract turn from the surface.

“I think spin is going to be key. Some of the Bangladeshi guys were getting some turn, and they were able to create some quiet periods in the match. But it’s just a matter of the mindset and how the other guys approach it. Pacers, spinners, everybody has their fair share to do tomorrow,” he said.
